metadata.title: Does all work and no play make elite students? Evidence from the China education panel survey

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the China Education Panel Survey (CEPS) baseline (2013–2014 school year) with a multistage sampling design: 28 counties/city districts, 112 schools, and 438 classes across China. The paper reports a representative national sample and includes school fixed effects and standard errors clustered at the class level, but it does not report the use of explicit student/sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the analysis is based on generalized propensity score matching and regression-based dose-response estimation (not PV-based ILSA scaling), the manuscript does not specify any PV-weighting or ILSA weight variables. Therefore, survey weights are not documented; readers should treat the causal estimates as conditional on the reported covariate adjustment and the sampling design, rather than as fully weight-adjusted population estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is constructed from CEPS school midterm exam standardized scores (Chinese, mathematics, English) and from questionnaire-based mediators (learning difficulty and self-efficacy), not from ILSA cognitive achievement plausible values. As a result, plausible-value handling is not applicable to this study’s outcome construction. The manuscript does not describe how missing questionnaire responses or missing covariates were handled (e.g., complete-case vs. imputation), which is a reporting gap because the tables show different observation counts across models.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses CEPS baseline data (2013–2014 school year) for two cohorts of middle school students in 7th and 9th grades. The paper reports 19,487 baseline samples collected from 28 county-level administrative units/city districts, 112 schools, and 438 classes. Analytic samples vary by model (e.g., Table 1 shows observation counts for learning-time variables and Table 3 shows 10,547/7,456 for weekday mechanisms), implying that cases with missing values on key variables (after-class learning time, mediators, or covariates) were excluded, but the exact missing-data rule is not explicitly stated.

main_findings.dataset_used: CEPS 2013-2014 (China) Grade 7/9 Midterm standardized scores (Chinese, Mathematics, English)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Generalized propensity score matching dose-response (inverted U). OLS (Table 2): weekday linear term not significant without quadratic; with quadratic, weekday linear positive and quadratic negative; weekend linear positive and quadratic negative. Reported R² (OLS): 0.255–0.260; clustered SE at class level.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using CEPS 2013–2014 Grade 7/9 the study leveraged after-class learning time (weekday and weekend, modeled with linear and quadratic terms) alongside student background controls such as gender, household registration, grade, only-child status, cognitive ability, parents’ education/occupation, head teacher title, and class quality to predict total academic performance. It found a relatively stable “inverted U” causal relationship, with best performance around 3 hours/day on weekdays and 8 hours/day on weekends, and that learning beyond these points hinders achievement. This indicates that policies should target an evidence-based “optimal” homework/tutoring time window rather than promoting maximal after-school study time, while recognizing that the estimates rely on observational causal assumptions (generalized propensity score matching) rather than randomized assignment.

main_findings.dataset_used: CEPS 2013-2014 (China) Grade 7/9 Midterm standardized scores (Chinese, Mathematics, English)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mediation model (Table 3, weekdays): For appropriate learning time (<=3h), LT on weekdays → learning difficulty coefficient 0.057*** (SE 0.019); learning difficulty → test score coefficient −4.034*** (SE 0.113). For excessive learning time (>3h), LT on weekdays → learning difficulty coefficient 0.020*** (SE 0.006); learning difficulty → test score coefficient −3.970*** (SE 0.136). Mediating effect proportions: 10.21% (appropriate) and 19.17% (excessive).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using CEPS 2013–2014 Grade 7/9 the study leveraged weekday after-class learning time (split into appropriate <=3h and excessive >3h) and student background controls to predict learning difficulty and then its effect on total academic performance. It found that appropriate learning time significantly decreases learning difficulty, whereas excessive learning time significantly increases learning difficulty, and that learning difficulty mediates a meaningful share of the total effect (10.21% for appropriate vs 19.17% for excessive). This indicates that interventions should not only regulate time but also monitor students’ perceived difficulty, because time beyond the optimal window may harm achievement by worsening learning difficulty perceptions.

main_findings.dataset_used: CEPS 2013-2014 (China) Grade 7/9 Midterm standardized scores (Chinese, Mathematics, English)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mediation model (Table 3, weekdays): For appropriate learning time (<=3h), LT on weekdays → self-efficacy coefficient 2.235*** (SE 0.228) and self-efficacy → test score coefficient 4.982*** (SE 0.309). For excessive learning time (>3h), LT on weekdays → self-efficacy coefficient −0.005*** (SE 0.002) and self-efficacy → test score coefficient 4.512*** (SE 0.374). Mediating effect proportions: 6.99% (appropriate) and 5.38% (excessive).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using CEPS 2013–2014 Grade 7/9 the study leveraged weekday after-class learning time (<=3h vs >3h) and background controls to predict self-efficacy and then its effect on total academic performance. It found that appropriate learning time increases self-efficacy and excessive learning time decreases self-efficacy, with self-efficacy mediating 6.99% of the total effect for appropriate time and 5.38% for excessive time. This indicates that after-school learning policies should emphasize sustainable, confidence-building study routines within an optimal time window, because overly long schedules may undermine achievement by eroding students’ self-efficacy.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses CEPS baseline data from the 2013–2014 school year for middle school students in Grades 7 and 9 in China (N=19,487; sampled via 28 county-level units/city districts, 112 schools, and 438 classes). Academic performance is measured as standardized midterm exam scores in Chinese, mathematics, and English, summed into a total test score. Using generalized propensity score matching and a dose-response (dose-response function) approach, the authors estimate a stable “inverted U” causal pattern: best performance occurs at about 3 hours/day on weekdays and 8 hours/day on weekends, while longer study time hinders achievement. Mediation analyses show that the effect operates through perceived learning difficulty and self-efficacy, with meaningful mediated proportions (e.g., 10.21%/19.17% for learning difficulty and 6.99%/5.38% for self-efficacy on weekdays). Limitations include lack of explicit missing-data handling documentation and reliance on observational causal assumptions rather than randomized assignment.
